w: What's tested The five translocations he said you need: t(14;18) follicular, t(11;14) mantle cell (a cyclin D1 stain means mantle cell), t(8;14) Burkitt, t(9;22) CML, t(15;17) APL Which lymphomas are B-cell and which T-cell, which are slow and which fast, and Hodgkin versus the rest Acute leukemia: blasts, more than 20 percent; Auer rods mean myeloid; AML in adults, ALL in children; APL (bleeding, a great cure) and acute monocytic leukemia in the gums CML, the chronic leukemia to know, and CLL with its smudge cells The B symptoms, and what these diseases look like in the mouth Dr. Borak's lecture on Tuesday, November 17, covers the blood cancers: lymphomas, which start in the lymph system, and leukemias, which start in the marrow. He said not to freak out about the amount of detail: know the basics, each disease's category and its translocation. You don't need the CD markers or the flow cytometry details. These notes follow the recording and slides. How blood cells mature Every blood cell comes from a stem cell in the marrow, down a myeloid line (red cells, platelets, neutrophils, monocytes) or a lymphoid line (B, T and NK cells). Mostly the white cells turn cancerous: the myeloid ones mostly into leukemias, the lymphoid ones into lymphomas or leukemias. A neutrophil grows up in this order: myeloblast, promyelocyte (granules appear), myelocyte, metamyelocyte, band, segmented neutrophil. The blast is the youngest. In leukemia the cells get stuck young, and blasts pile up. Blasts in the blood are never normal, except in a newborn. What a lymphoma is A lymphoma is a cancer of lymphocytes, and it can start in lymph tissue almost anywhere. You need a piece of tissue, a node or marrow, to diagnose it; he likes to take out the whole node. Big nodes aren't always lymphoma: infections and diseases like lupus swell them too. The B symptoms He called them high-yield clues: a fever of 38 degrees Celsius or more, night sweats that soak the sheets, and losing at least 10 percent of your weight in 6 months without trying. Tuberculosis can do this too, so you still need the tissue. The tissue and flow cytometry A normal node is rubbery, with follicles in its outer layer and open channels (sinuses). A lymphoma node is fleshy, and its normal pattern is wiped out by one kind of cell. The lab looks at the cells (the H and E stain), stains the tissue with antibodies, and runs flow cytometry, which tells B cell, T cell or myeloid, young or mature. Each B cell carries kappa or lambda; a normal node has both, but a lymphoma's cells all carry just one, because they are one clone. Send the tissue for flow fresh, not in formalin, in a medium like RPMI or Hanks's solution, because flow needs living cells. Flow shines a laser through cells one at a time: forward scatter tells the size, side scatter tells how grainy the cell is. He said not to spend a second on the CD markers. Classifying lymphoma It takes everything together, but how the cells look matters most. Most lymphomas, 85 to 90 percent, are B-cell. Most of the rest are T-cell; NK-cell ones are rare. Each comes from a normal cell: the follicle's center gives follicular lymphoma, the rim around it (the mantle) gives mantle cell lymphoma, and the zone outside that gives marginal zone lymphoma. Lymphoma near the mouth and eye Lymphoma can start in the eye (painless blurry vision or floaters, or a puffy, salmon-colored swelling beside the eye), the tonsils (very swollen), and the gums (a flat or ulcerated patch rather than a lump). Hodgkin versus the rest Hodgkin lymphoma is usually found in one area. It starts in nodes deep in the chest, spreads node to node in order, rarely leaves the nodes and never gets into the blood, and its cancer cells are a few big, odd-looking cells. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is usually widespread when found, can skip nodes, often starts outside them, can get into the blood, and its cells look like normal lymphocytes. They are treated differently. Staging Staging asks how far it has spread: one place or several, above the diaphragm, below it or both, outside the nodes, or everywhere. Everywhere is stage 4, the worst. B means B symptoms. What leukemia is Lymphoma is mostly in nodes; leukemia is mostly in the marrow and blood. Leukemia is cancer cells taking over the marrow and blood. It starts in the marrow and can spread to the spleen, liver and nodes. Untreated, it kills. It hurts you two ways. The marrow fails: anemia (tired, pale), low platelets (bruising, bleeding) and too few good white cells (fever, infections). And the cells move into organs: bone pain, a big spleen and liver, big nodes, nerve problems, and swollen gums. He said a dentist may be the first to spot a leukemia this way. The marrow exam A blood count flags the blasts, a smear confirms them, then the marrow is sampled, numbed first. The back of the hip bone (posterior iliac crest) gives both a core biopsy and an aspirate. The sternum gives an aspirate only (the heart is right under it), and so does the tibia in small children. Acute versus chronic Acute: blasts over 20 percent, a fast start, death in under 6 months without treatment, very low platelets, mildly enlarged organs. Chronic myeloid: mature cells, under 20 percent blasts, a slow start, 2 to 6 years without treatment, platelets normal or high at first, a big spleen. Both kill by infection or bleeding. AML and ALL He said acute leukemia is mostly children for ALL, but adults for AML (median age 65). ALL is mostly in small children, usually 1 to 5, and does badly under age 1. Myeloblasts are bigger, with granules and sometimes Auer rods. Lymphoblasts are smaller, with little cytoplasm and no granules. An Auer rod means it isn't ALL. The number: more than 20 percent blasts makes the diagnosis. If the AML has one of its defining genetic changes, the blast count doesn't matter. You don't need the AML subtypes. Indolent or aggressive He wants you to know each lymphoma's group. Slow B-cell: CLL/SLL, follicular, mantle cell, marginal zone. Fast B-cell: diffuse large B-cell, Burkitt. T-cell: mycosis fungoides (slow), Sézary syndrome, peripheral T-cell and NK/T-cell lymphoma (fast). Hodgkin and the plasma cell tumors are groups of their own. CLL/SLL Small, mature B cells in older people (median 70 or older). Called CLL when there are at least 5,000 per microliter of these B cells in the blood, SLL when it is mostly in the nodes. Same disease. Fewer than that, with no node disease, is a pre-cancer called monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis. On the smear: "soccer ball" chromatin and smudge cells. Infections come from low antibodies. It is slow but mostly incurable. Follicular lymphoma Crowded, back-to-back follicles. The translocation t(14;18) keeps BCL2 on, so the cells don't die. Usually widespread when found, but often without symptoms. Slow: median survival over 17 years. Mantle cell lymphoma From the mantle zone around the follicle. Small to medium cells with irregular nuclei and the translocation t(11;14), which nothing else has. He said if a question says the cells stain for cyclin D1, it's mantle cell lymphoma. Older patients (median 68 to 69) with big nodes. Survival has gotten much better. MALT lymphoma The one dentists will see most, he said: a slow B-cell lymphoma, often outside the nodes, grown out of long inflammation, with tumor cells invading the gland's lining. The stomach with H. pylori, the skin with Borrelia, the eye area with Chlamydia psittaci, the salivary gland after Sjögren syndrome, the thyroid after Hashimoto thyroiditis. Some respond to antibiotics. Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma Big B cells in sheets: about 30 percent of adult lymphomas. A node or mass that grows fast; 30 to 40 percent start outside the nodes (stomach, salivary glands, thyroid, bone). It grows fast, can start on its own or grow out of a slow lymphoma, and often brings B symptoms. About 70 percent are doing well at 5 years after R-CHOP. Burkitt lymphoma Very fast-growing B cells. The translocation t(8;14) turns on MYC. Under the microscope: a starry sky, pale macrophages eating dead tumor cells among blue tumor cells. The starry sky is the key finding. Endemic (equatorial Africa, Papua New Guinea): children, the jaws, EBV in over 90 percent. Sporadic (everywhere else): the abdomen, gums and tonsils, EBV in about 20 percent. (Once, aloud, he swapped the two names; his slide and the textbooks say it this way.) Also seen with HIV. Jaw pain and loose teeth can be the first sign. Treatment works very well: about 90 percent of children survive. Hodgkin lymphoma A few big Reed-Sternberg cells ("owl's eyes") in a crowd of normal immune cells: he said they are the main thing to recognize. It stays in nodes above the diaphragm (the neck, above the collarbone, the chest) and spreads node to node in order. Painless, firm nodes; rarely, node pain after alcohol. Starting outside the nodes is rare. Nodular sclerosis has bands of scar tissue; you don't need the differences between the types. EBV drives some cases. Over 80 percent are cured. The other lymphomas (non-Hodgkin) more often start outside the nodes and are more often widespread when found. Plasma cell tumors A plasmacytoma is one tumor of plasma cells, often in a rib or the spine. Multiple myeloma is plasma cells all through the marrow, making one antibody (the M-spike), with organ damage: CRAB, for high calcium, kidney damage, anemia and holes in the bones. Red cells stack like coins (rouleaux) because of all that antibody. Myeloma is usually incurable. T-cell lymphoma He skipped peripheral T-cell lymphoma, saying only: very aggressive, B symptoms, and chemotherapy often doesn't work. Mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome He went through these quickly. Mycosis fungoides is the most common lymphoma of the skin, and slow: skin patches, then plaques, then tumors, often in the "bathing trunk" area. Sézary syndrome: red skin all over, big nodes and the same cells (with brain-shaped nuclei) in the blood; aggressive. Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma It starts in the nose, destroys vessels and tissue, and can punch a hole in the hard palate. Strongly linked to EBV; mostly in eastern Asia and Indigenous peoples of Central and South America. CML The chronic leukemia he said you need. The Philadelphia chromosome, t(9;22), makes BCR-ABL1, an enzyme stuck on. Most people are found in the slow chronic phase, sometimes by a routine blood count. The white count is very high (median about 80,000 per microliter), mostly neutrophils of every age, not blasts, and the spleen is big. Untreated, it turns into a blast phase in a few years. Imatinib (Gleevec) blocks the enzyme by taking ATP's place. Blasts and Auer rods Blasts mean acute leukemia, but a few (under 20 percent) can show up in MDS too. After the newborn period, any blast in the blood is abnormal. Auer rods are red-blue needles inside myeloblasts: an Auer rod means the blast is myeloid, never ALL. APL One of the two acute leukemias he said you need. A type of AML where the cells get stuck as promyelocytes, full of big granules and bundles of Auer rods. The translocation t(15;17) joins PML and RARA. The danger is DIC, clotting and bleeding all at once: bleeding gums, bruises, and early death. Retinoic acid with arsenic cures most. Acute monocytic leukemia The other acute leukemia he said you need, for one reason: it can show up in the mouth. An AML of monocyte-like cells with kidney-shaped nuclei. It can grow in the gums (myeloid sarcoma) and make them swell. Swollen gums in someone tired, pale and bruising: get a blood count. B-ALL and T-ALL For these he said you only need who gets them. B-ALL is the most common leukemia in children (75 percent are under 6), with a smaller second peak in the 40s. It shows as marrow failure. Over 90 percent of children do well. T-ALL looks the same under the microscope (tests show the T cells), and does a little worse; it often has a high white count and a mass in the chest, and the lymphoma form can block the airway. Where acute leukemia comes from Some acute leukemias start on their own. Others are the end of another marrow disease (MDS, CML, CMML, or a myeloproliferative neoplasm: polycythemia vera with too many red cells, essential thrombocythemia with too many platelets, myelofibrosis with a scarred marrow). It can come within 10 years of chemotherapy or radiation for another cancer, with a bad prognosis. And it can come with Down syndrome. Treatment Kill the leukemia (chemotherapy, radiation, transplant) and support the patient. The goal is complete remission: no symptoms, no disease found, normal blood counts. The translocations He said you do need these. t(14;18), BCL2 Follicular lymphoma t(11;14), cyclin D1 Mantle cell lymphoma t(8;14), MYC Burkitt lymphoma t(9;22), BCR-ABL1 (Philadelphia) CML t(15;17), PML-RARA APL In the mouth Swollen gums: AML in the gums. Bleeding gums and spots: low platelets, or DIC in APL. A fast jaw mass in a child: Burkitt. A hole in the palate: NK/T-cell lymphoma. A new parotid lump with Sjögren: MALT lymphoma. Punched-out holes in the jaw with high calcium: myeloma.
